v: Calgary's avenues once had names, not numbers.
In early eighteen eighty-four, the Canadian Pacific Railway registered the townsite of Calgary, and named its streets and avenues after company officials.
Vice-presidents Angus and McIntyre. Director Smith. General manager Van Horne. They were the original namesakes of today's Sixth, Seventh, Eleventh and Twelfth Avenues.
The main commercial road was Stephen Avenue, named for the railway's first president.
And today's Ninth Avenue Southeast was once known as Atlantic Avenue, and as Whisky Row. It was Calgary's first main street.
Then, in nineteen oh four, bylaw number five twenty-eight changed the avenue names to numbers.
Stephen Avenue became Eighth Avenue. But for a few years, ads and newspapers kept using the old name too.
Today, avenues run east and west. Streets run north and south.
Roughly speaking, Centre Street splits the city east from west, and the Bow River splits it north from south. That makes four quadrants.
So the quadrant matters. The same address can exist in more than one quadrant. Leave it off, and you could end up on the wrong side of the city.
And here's the twist. Centre Street and Centre Avenue don't meet in the middle of downtown, as you might expect. In theory, they cross in the middle of the Centre Street Bridge.
Even the downtown avenues aren't true east and west. They run parallel to the railway tracks.
As for Stephen Avenue, its name came back in nineteen eighty-one, on the pedestrian mall.
